LESSON 29 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

Public-Key Cryptography and Key Exchange

How a public and private key pair replaces a shared secret, how an ephemeral exchange produces a session key, and which two things it still does not authenticate.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Public-key cryptography uses a mathematically linked pair of keys: one that can be published and one that cannot. It solved the key distribution problem that had limited symmetric encryption for decades.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Each user holds a private key that stays with them and a public key that anyone can have.
  • Data encrypted to your public key can only be decrypted with your private key.
  • A signature created with your private key can be verified by anyone holding your public key.
  • A key agreement protocol such as Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive one shared secret over an observed channel, without ever sending the secret.
  • The security rests on a mathematical problem being hard in one direction and easy in the other, which is why only reviewed curves and parameters are acceptable.

The background

  • Public-key ideas appeared in classified work in the 1970s and were published by Diffie, Hellman and Rivest.
  • RSA became the dominant scheme for both encryption and signatures, and for a long time was also used with small parameters by mistake.
  • Elliptic-curve schemes offer equivalent strength with much smaller keys, which reduced handshake cost and is now the default in TLS.
  • Post-quantum schemes have been standardised for the future, because an adversary can record traffic today and decrypt it later.

Real-world examples

  • A key exchange with a non-standard curve removes the assumption that discrete logarithms are hard, which can let an attacker recover the shared secret.
  • Traffic captured today can be decrypted in future if the algorithm used is broken later, which is why harvest-now-decrypt-later is a real concern.
  • An implementation that accepts any offered parameter can be coerced into choosing a weak one.

What to look for

  • Confirm only standard curves and standard parameter sizes are accepted, with no negotiation downgrade path.
  • Check that keys are generated with a good random source rather than derived from predictable values.
  • Notice whether forward secrecy is claimed, since it decides whether a later key compromise exposes old traffic.
  • Check that key validation actually happens, since an unauthenticated handshake has no identity to trust.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use well-reviewed algorithms from a maintained library, and avoid implementing the mathematics yourself.
  • Enable forward secrecy, commonly called ephemeral key exchange, so past traffic is not exposed by a later key theft.
  • Pin the set of acceptable parameters in configuration rather than trusting the peer to choose.
  • Plan a migration path to post-quantum key exchange for long-lived sensitive traffic.
  • Validate peer keys against something you already trust rather than accepting whatever is presented.
